title: Greg Brockman walks back a planned second $25M donation to Leading the Future
subtitle: OpenAI's president told employees in a June Slack message he felt 'terrible' about the pro-AI super PAC's reflection on the company — and now, with midterms approaching, the backing stops at $25 million instead of $50 million.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife Anna originally pledged a combined $50 million to Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC positioning for the November midterms. According to reporting from Benzinga, Gizmodo and the New York Times picked up October 1 and 2, Brockman has delivered the first $25 million but will not deliver the second. In a June Slack message to employees, he wrote that he felt 'terrible' about the way the PAC 'keeps reflecting on the company' and that he and Anna had 'no plans to donate more at this time.' OpenAI stated in June that Brockman's involvement was personal, not corporate. By July, rank-and-file OpenAI staff had contributed more than $200,000 to a counterweight super PAC.

This is OpenAI's first visible political fracture that is not about safety governance or model release decisions. Leading the Future was built to push candidates sympathetic to minimal AI regulation and to oppose candidates aligned with the EU-style precautionary posture. The arithmetic of a $50 million versus a $25 million budget is not trivial — it is roughly the difference between competitive statewide ad buys in multiple swing races and a single national-media buy. More consequential is the signal: a founding executive publicly stepped back from an advocacy vehicle associated with his own industry, citing company reputation rather than policy disagreement.

The timing matters. The FTC opened a broad consumer-protection investigation into frontier labs on October 1. The White House super-intelligence accord, in which six CEOs including Brockman's colleagues at OpenAI agreed to self-police, was signed September 30. A super PAC pushing a maximalist pro-industry line in that context creates friction with the self-regulation story the labs are now trying to tell Washington. Brockman's pullback reads as reputation management in a moment when the industry is being asked to look restrained.

For learners interested in policy: the AI industry's internal political strategy is now a legitimate subject of study, separate from the technology. Who funds which super PACs, which executives sign which open letters, and which labs break ranks on which bills — these are the levers that will shape the regulatory environment you will work in. Follow Leading the Future and its counterweight PACs the same way you follow benchmark scores. The money is where the policy actually gets decided.
